system:
You are an experienced litigator who has supervised many document reviews. You
are asked to estimate, item by item, how hard it is for a human reviewer to
check one call, and to say why.

### The reviewer's task

The reviewer is law-trained but not a specialist in the case's industry, and
**has already read and understood this case**: the opinion, the contracts, and
every court defect — each provision the court construed, and for each one every
distinct defect the court construed in it, with the passage of the opinion it
comes from.

They are now given a list of **items**. Each item is one description of a
defect, written by someone else about one provision the court construed, and
the call a first reader made on it. The call is one of two kinds:

- **A match.** The first reader said the description names one particular court
  defect on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether it does — whether
  the description and that court defect are about the same words and the same
  problem with them — and not some other court defect, or none.
- **No match.** The first reader said the description names none of the court
  defects on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether that is right —
  whether the description fails to name each one of them.

You are judging **how hard it is to reach that decision** for each item. Not
whether the first reader was right: do not decide that, and do not let a view
on it set the difficulty. Not how hard the case is: the reviewer already knows
the case, so count only the work this item adds.

### What does not count

- **How hard the case is.** Two items in one case can differ widely. Rate each
  item by what checking it takes on top of an understanding of the case.
- **The number of items.** Each item is rated on its own, and an item does not
  get easier or harder because there are many others.
- **Length by itself.** A long description is hard only where its length makes
  it unclear what it names.
- **How close the description is to the court defect.** A full match, a clear
  partial match and a clear mismatch are all easy to check. Difficulty is how
  hard it is to **see** how close they are, not how close they turn out to be.
- **Wording.** A description that calls the court's problem by another name —
  "indefinite" where the court said "ambiguous", "open-ended" where it said
  "unclear" — about the same words is no harder to check than one that uses
  the court's own word.
- **Distinctions the court did not draw.** Two framings of what is wrong with
  the same words — its meaning is uncertain, its reach is too broad — can be
  told apart in theory. A reviewer does not stop over that unless **the court's
  construction turned on it**: unless the court accepted one framing and
  rejected the other, or decided the case on a point one framing reaches and
  the other misses. Where the court did not, the reviewer sees the same words
  and the same kind of complaint, and confirms the call at a glance.

### How a reviewer actually checks an item

To check an item the reviewer has to settle, in turn:

1. **What the description is about** — which words, which other provision or
   document, and what it says is wrong with them;
2. **whether each thing it asserts is true** — what the contract says, what a
   term or a document is, what happened between the parties;
3. **whether that is what the court construed** — the same words, and the
   point the court's construction actually turned on;
4. **whether the call follows** — given all that, does the description name the
   matched court defect, or none of them.

An item is easy when every step is quick and the answer to each is plain. It is
hard when a step cannot be finished from the clause and the passage, or when,
with every step done, it is still not plain what the answer is.

### What makes an item easy to check

The comparison is clear-cut, whichever way it comes out:

- **One phrase, one step.** The description points at a phrase of the clause
  and says what is wrong with it in one step — this phrase is vague, this term
  is undefined — and the court construed that phrase for that reason. The
  reviewer reads the description once and confirms it against the passage.
- **Plainly different.** The description is about other words, or a different
  problem, so the mismatch is seen just as quickly.
- **Anything extra is plainly separate.** Where the description also raises a
  point about another clause, term or objection, that point is set aside at a
  glance; it does not need to be checked to decide the call.
- **Nothing to verify.** What the description asserts can be seen in the
  clause and the passage themselves.
- **The provision has one court defect**, or its court defects are clearly
  separate, so there is only one comparison to make.

An item like that takes a minute or two, and the reviewer ends confident.

### What makes an item hard to check

What makes an item hard is that **a step cannot be settled from the clause and
the passage, or the answer stays unclear once it is**. Each of these adds time,
and they compound:

- **The two sides may name the same thing differently.** The description
  refers to a document, a party, a transaction or a category of things by one
  name, and the court by another, and whether they are the same thing is a
  question of fact — about the deal, the record or the industry — that the
  reviewer has to look up before the comparison can even start.
- **The description makes claims that have to be verified.** It asserts facts
  about the contract, the parties, a court or a body, a document or the
  background, and the reviewer has to check them against the contract, the
  opinion or outside knowledge. Some may turn out to be wrong.
- **It bundles several claims about the same defect, some of them doubtful.**
  The description makes several points about the same words or the same
  dispute; some look right and some look wrong. The reviewer has to grade each
  and then decide whether the call stands on the right ones.
- **It has the right words but not the court's point.** The description is
  about the words the court construed, but misses, or misstates, a point the
  court's construction actually turned on — one the opinion relies on, not one
  a reader could merely imagine. The reviewer has to decide whether that still
  names the court defect, and even with every fact checked, careful reviewers
  can disagree.
- **Its reasoning runs over several steps.** The description reaches its defect
  through a chain — this term, read with that provision, given this fact — and
  the reviewer has to follow and test each link.
- **The defect is relational and the description has only part of it.** The
  court's defect lies in how this provision is read with another provision or
  with a separate document, and the description addresses only this one, or
  only one side of the relationship, so the reviewer has to decide how much of
  the relationship it must reach before it counts.
- **The description is vague or general.** It could be read as naming the court
  defect or as naming something near it, and the reviewer has to decide how
  much it must say before it counts.
- **Several court defects on the provision are close to one another**, so the
  description could name one, another, or more than one of them, and the
  reviewer has to tell them apart before they can check the call.

An item like that can take half an hour or more, and the reviewer may still be
unsure at the end.

### The scale

- **`difficulty`** — `easy`, `intermediate` or `hard`.
- **`score`** — an integer from 1 to 10, and use the whole range. 1–3 is easy:
  1–2 when the decision is plain at a glance, 3 when one more look is needed.
  4–6 is intermediate: a claim to verify or a framing to work through, but the
  answer is plain once that is done. 7–10 is hard: 9–10 when, with every claim
  checked, two careful reviewers could still decide it differently.
  `difficulty` and `score` must agree.
- **`estimated_minutes`** — your estimate of how long the reviewer needs to
  reach a decision on this item, given that they already understand the case.
  Count only the work this item adds.
instructions:
Work in this order.

1. **Read the court defects** in the task and the provisions they sit in, until
   you could say what each one is about in a sentence.
2. **Go through the items one at a time.** For each one, read the description,
   then the court defects on its provision, then the call, and walk the four
   steps a reviewer takes: what the description is about, whether what it
   asserts is true, whether that is what the court construed, whether the call
   follows. Note which step takes work, what that work needs — the clause, the
   rest of the contract, the opinion, outside facts — and whether its answer is
   plain once the work is done.
3. **Rate the item by how clear that comparison is** — not by how close the
   description turns out to be, not by how hard the case is, and not by whether
   you think the call is right.

Return exactly one entry per item, under its id, in the order given.

In each `reason`, give one or two sentences specific to this item: name the
step that takes the work, and the words, claim or court defect it turns on.
task:
### The court defects in 161 F.Supp.3d 970

### Contract 161FSupp3d970_policy_of_insurance_number

#### c009 — Insuring Agreement

```
Insuring Agreement Subject to all the terms and conditions of this policy, we will pay for risks of direct physical loss or damage to covered property as a result of an occurrence, unless excluded.
```

- **d01** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): The phrase “direct physical loss or damage” was alleged to be lexically ambiguous between any physical alteration, including cosmetic hail dents, and only damage measurably reducing the property’s usefulness or function.
  Opinion lines 28-30:
```
Plaintiff argues that the Advance Cable case demonstrates that “physical loss or damage” language in an insurance policy unambiguously applies to cosmetic hail dents. Defendant attempts to distinguish Advance Cable based on the different policy language in that case. In Advance Cable, the policy expressly defined “direct physical ‘loss’ ” as “accidental loss or damage.” Here, the policy does not define “loss” as “loss or damage,” and the word “damage” is not included at all in the “Coverages” section. Defendant argues that because of these distinctions, the interpretation of “loss or damage” in Advance Cable does not apply to this case.
Based on a plain reading of the phrase “physical loss or damage,” the Court finds that the “Insuring Agreement” section of the Policy unambiguously provides coverage for hail dents on a metal seam roof. Here, the “Insuring Agreement” section states that Defendant will pay for risks of “physical loss or damage.” The court in Advance Cable held that this precise language provided coverage for cosmetic hail dents in an insured’s metal roofs. The distinction that Defendant draws between the language of this Policy and that in Advance Cable does not require the Court to ignore the interpretation of the phrase “loss or damage” in that case. Looking beyond Advance Cable, the phrase “physical damage” in an insurance policy is widely accepted to mean a “physical alteration.” Thus, the Court finds that the phrase “physical loss or damage” provides coverage where, as here, cosmetic hail dents physically alter an insured’s property.
Defendant cites several cases for the proposition that “physical loss or damage” requires a showing of a measurable reduction in the property’s usefulness or a change to an unsatisfactory state. These cases, however, do not apply directly to the interpretation of the phrase “physical loss or damage” in this Policy. Against the backdrop of Advance Cable and other persuasive authority that suggests that “physical loss or damage” includes cosmetic hail damage that physically alters an insured’s property, the Court is not convinced that the cases offered by Defendant define the phrase to mean functional damage. At best, Defendant’s authority provides a competing interpretation for “physical loss or damage,” thereby creating ambiguity as to whether this phrase encompasses cosmetic damage. Such an ambiguity would result in the Court interpreting the phrase in Plaintiffs favor to include cosmetic damage. However, the Court has found above that based on a plain and ordinary reading of the “Insuring Agreement” section, the phrase “physical loss or damage” unambiguously includes the cosmetic hail damage to Plaintiffs Covered Property.
```

- **d02** (risk type 1.3, scope `contract`): The general “physical loss or damage” grant was alleged under ejusdem generis to be narrowed by the supposedly more specific real-property “covered loss” provisions, creating a general-versus-specific scope problem even though no specific enumeration preceded the general grant.
  Opinion lines 33-33:
```
Defendant argues that the more specific definition of “covered loss” in the “Coverages” section acts as a limitation on the “physical loss or damage” language in the “Insuring Agreement” section. Defendant invokes the rule of ejusdem generis, arguing that under this principle the Policy’s more specific provisions in the “Coverages” section control over the more general provisions at the beginning of the Policy in the “Insuring Agreement” section. Defendant confuses the meaning of this maxim. Ejusdem generis applies in the context of ambiguous contracts where an enumeration of specific things is followed by a more general word or phrase, and the general word or phrase is held to refer to things of the same kind enumerated. Lack of ambiguity aside, here the general “Insuring Agreement” section is not preceded by a specific enumeration of coverage limitations, as required to trigger the application of ejusdem generis. Thus, Defendant’s argument must be construed as promoting the phrase “covered loss” as a limitation on the general “Insuring Agreement” clause in the context of real property claims.
```

#### c029 — A. Real Property coverage

```
COVERAGES A. Ifcoverage for real property is provided as shown in B, Coverages of the DECLARATIONS, Fortin RM1000. we will pay for a covered loss to your real property at or within onc-thousand (1,000) feet of acovered location.
```

- **d03** (risk type 1.1, scope `contract`): The phrase “covered loss” in the real-property coverage grant was alleged to be lexically ambiguous between requiring functional or financial loss and encompassing cosmetic dents as an undesirable outcome or financial detriment.
  Opinion lines 32-34:
```
The Court next turns to the- “Coverages” section of the Policy. Defendant argues that because Plaintiffs claim involves real property, the scope of coverage under the Policy is defined not by the “Insuring Agreement” section, but by the “Coverages” section. This section states that “[i]f coverage for real property is provided ... we will pay for a covered loss to your real property at or within one-thousand (1,000) feet of a covered location.” Defendant points to the definition of “covered loss” in the Policy as “a loss to covered property at a covered location resulting from a peril insured against.” Defendant cites several cases and dictionary definitions for the proposition that “a loss” means “an undesirable outcome of a risk” or a “financial detriment.” Based on these definitions, Defendant argues, the Policy unambiguously requires a showing of functional damage to establish a loss.
Defendant argues that the more specific definition of “covered loss” in the “Coverages” section acts as a limitation on the “physical loss or damage” language in the “Insuring Agreement” section. Defendant invokes the rule of ejusdem generis, arguing that under this principle the Policy’s more specific provisions in the “Coverages” section control over the more general provisions at the beginning of the Policy in the “Insuring Agreement” section. Defendant confuses the meaning of this maxim. Ejusdem generis applies in the context of ambiguous contracts where an enumeration of specific things is followed by a more general word or phrase, and the general word or phrase is held to refer to things of the same kind enumerated. Lack of ambiguity aside, here the general “Insuring Agreement” section is not preceded by a specific enumeration of coverage limitations, as required to trigger the application of ejusdem generis. Thus, Defendant’s argument must be construed as promoting the phrase “covered loss” as a limitation on the general “Insuring Agreement” clause in the context of real property claims.
According to Defendant, “the Policy language specific to real property, contained within the ‘COVERAGES’ form of the Policy, controls over any broad and general language of the insuring agreement.” As a general rule, limitations, exclusions, and exceptions in insurance policies are construed narrowly, and the insurer assumes the burden to define limitations in clear and specific terms. Failure of an insurer to define limitations unambiguously “will result in strict construction against the insurer.” Defendant argues that because courts have defined “a loss” as an “undesirable outcome” or “financial detriment,” the phrase requires an actual functional loss to the property. Plaintiff cites authority suggesting that even cosmetic hail dents create an “undesirable outcome” or a “financial detriment.” Based on this competing authority, the Court finds that the phrase “covered loss” does not unambiguously limit coverage of real property to functional damage. Thus, the “Insuring Agreement” section, which unambiguously allows for coverage of cosmetic hail damage, is not limited by the “covered loss” language in the “Coverages” section. Accordingly, the Court grants Plaintiff summary judgment on the issue of whether the Policy provides coverage for hail indentations to the metal roofs of the Covered Property.
```

- **d04** (risk type 1.3, scope `contract`): The real-property grant’s allegedly more specific “covered loss” wording was asserted to control the general “physical loss or damage” grant under ejusdem generis, although the policy lacked the required specific enumeration followed by general language.
  Opinion lines 33-33:
  The same passage as d02 above.

#### c215 — F. Covered loss

```
Covered loss means a loss to covered property at a covered location resulting from a peril insured against.
```

- **d05** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): The undefined words “a loss” within the “covered loss” definition were alleged to be lexically ambiguous between an outcome requiring functional damage and an undesirable outcome or financial detriment that could include cosmetic hail dents.
  Opinion lines 32-34:
  The same passage as d03 above.

- **d06** (risk type 1.3, scope `contract`): The “covered loss” definition was asserted to be the specific provision limiting the broader general grant of “physical loss or damage,” but the court found no enumerated-list and general-term structure supporting ejusdem generis.
  Opinion lines 33-33:
  The same passage as d02 above.


### The items to rate

#### a01

On `161FSupp3d970_policy_of_insurance_number` c009 — Insuring Agreement. Court defects on this provision: d01, d02.

The description:
```
"Risks of direct physical loss or damage" is undefined and its boundary — whether cosmetic, functional or merely diminished-value harm counts as "direct physical loss or damage" — is the classic battleground of an all-risk grant. The phrase "unless excluded" also leaves the burden and reach of the exclusions to be worked out.
```

The first reader matched it to **d01**.

#### a02

On `161FSupp3d970_policy_of_insurance_number` c029 — A. Real Property coverage. Court defects on this provision: d03, d04.

The description:
```
The grant covers real property "at or within one-thousand (1,000) feet of a covered location," so its whole reach depends on the contested identification of covered locations under the Schedule (c028) and DEFINITIONS E. (c214). Property at an unlisted address may or may not fall within the grant.
```

The first reader matched it to **none** of d03, d04.

#### a03

On `161FSupp3d970_policy_of_insurance_number` c215 — F. Covered loss. Court defects on this provision: d05, d06.

The description:
```
"Covered loss" is confined to loss "at a covered location," although the Insuring Agreement (c009) and COVERAGES A. and B. (c029, c030) extend to property within 1,000 feet of, or in transit away from, a covered location. The definition and those grants describe different geographic reach.
```

The first reader matched it to **none** of d05, d06.

One entry per item above, each under its id.
